gh run list --limit 10
gh run view <run-id>
gh run watch

docs.title: Report Generation
docs.text: Generate professional Word documents with detection results and analysis.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The reporting feature creates branded Microsoft Word documents (.docx) containing:

  • Project Information: Name, description, creation date
  • Detection Statistics: Total images analyzed, detection rate, average confidence
  • Severity Breakdown: Distribution of crack severity levels
  • Sample Images: Representative detection results organized by severity
  • Anaxiatech Branding: Company logo, colors, and contact information

Reports are ideal for sharing inspection results with clients, stakeholders, or archival purposes.

docs.title: Basic Report Generation
docs.text:
Generate a report for your project:

crackz report generate --project demo-project

This creates demo-project_report.docx in the project directory.

docs.title: Custom Output Path
docs.text:
Specify where to save the report:

crackz report generate --project demo-project --output inspection_report.docx

docs.title: Using Config File
docs.text:
Generate from a YAML configuration:

crackz report generate --cfg project_config.yaml --output report.docx

docs.title: 1. Header Section
docs.text:
• Anaxiatech logo (automatically included if available)
  • Document title: "Harbor Infrastructure Inspection Report"
  • Subtitle: "Crack Detection Analysis"
  • Generation date: Timestamp when report was created

docs.title: 2. Project Information
docs.text: A table containing: - Project name - Description - Creation date

docs.title: 3. Detection Statistics
docs.text: Summary metrics including: - Total images analyzed - Number of images with detected cracks - Overall detection rate (%) - Average confidence level (%)

docs.title: 4. Severity Breakdown
docs.text:
Distribution of results by confidence level: - Crack Detected: High confidence detections (≥5% default) - Probable Crack: Medium confidence (2-5% default) - Possible Crack: Low confidence (0.5-2% default) - No Crack: Below detection threshold

Each severity level shows: - Number of images - Percentage of total - Color-coded for easy identification

docs.title: 5. Detection Results
docs.text:
Sample images organized by severity (up to 5 images per category): - Original filename - Detection visualization images with crack overlays and heatmaps - Confidence percentage - Crack area percentage (when available)

The report includes the actual detection visualization images showing: - Red/yellow overlay highlighting detected cracks - Color-coded intensity based on detection confidence - Visual representation of the AI's crack detection

Note: Images are automatically resized to fit page width while maintaining aspect ratio. Large image sets show a representative sample with a note about complete results.

docs.title: 6. Company Information
docs.text:
• About Anaxiatech section
  • Contact information (email, website)
  • Disclaimer about AI-generated results

docs.title: Severity Thresholds
docs.text:
Confidence thresholds are configured in your project's detection settings:

ai:
  detection:
    min_confidence: 0.005      # 0.5% - Possible Crack threshold
    medium_confidence: 0.02    # 2% - Probable Crack threshold
    high_confidence: 0.05      # 5% - Crack Detected threshold

Adjust these values to control how detections are categorized in reports.

docs.title: Image Limits
docs.text:
By default, reports include up to 5 sample images per severity level to keep file sizes manageable. This prevents extremely large documents when processing hundreds or thousands of images.

For complete results, refer to the project's detections/ directory.

docs.title: Client Deliverables
docs.text:
Share inspection results with harbor authorities or infrastructure managers: 

crackz report generate --project harbor_inspection_2024 \
  --output "Harbor_Inspection_Report_2024-Q4.docx"

docs.title: Progress Reports
docs.text:
Document ongoing monitoring campaigns: 

# Monthly reports
crackz report generate --project monthly_monitoring \
  --output "reports/2024-11_monitoring.docx"

docs.title: Compliance Documentation
docs.text:
Create records for regulatory compliance: 

crackz report generate --project compliance_check \
  --output "compliance/inspection_$(date +%Y%m%d).docx"

docs.title: Internal Reviews
docs.text:
Generate reports for internal quality assurance: 

crackz report generate --project qa_validation \
  --output "internal/qa_review.docx"

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
• Format: Microsoft Word (.docx) - Office 2007 and later
  • Compatibility: Microsoft Word, LibreOffice, Google Docs, Apple Pages
  • Styling: Professional theme with Anaxiatech brand colors
  • Images: Embedded at appropriate resolution (max 6 inches width)

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Detection must be run first (crackz detect run)
  • Detection results JSON must exist in project
  • Sufficient disk space for Word document (typically 5-50 MB depending on images)

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Report generation typically takes: - Small projects (10-50 images): 1-5 seconds - Medium projects (50-200 images): 5-15 seconds - Large projects (200+ images): 15-30 seconds

Large projects show only sample images to maintain reasonable generation times.

docs.title: No Detection Results
docs.text:
Problem: "No detection results found for project"

Solution: Run detection first: 

crackz detect run --project demo-project

docs.title: Images Not Appearing
docs.text:
Problem: Report shows "⚠️ Detection image not found" messages

Causes: - Detection visualizations were deleted or moved - Detection hasn't been run yet - Project directory structure is incorrect

Solution: Verify detection visualization images exist: 

# Check for visualization images (new structure)
ls -la demo-project/artifacts/detections/visualizations/

# Or legacy location (older projects)
ls -la demo-project/artifacts/detections/*.png

Re-run detection if needed: 

crackz detect run --project demo-project

Note: The report uses detection visualization images from artifacts/detections/visualizations/ which show the original images with crack overlays. These are automatically generated during detection.

docs.title: Large File Size
docs.text:
Problem: Report file is very large (>100 MB)

Cause: High-resolution detection images

Solutions: 1. The report automatically limits to 5 images per severity level 2. For smaller files, reduce detection image resolution in project config: 

data:
  size: [512, 512]  # Use smaller images

docs.title: Permission Denied
docs.text:
Problem: Cannot save report file

Solutions: - Check write permissions on output directory - Close the file if it's open in Word or another application - Specify a different output path with --output

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
Use descriptive, dated filenames: 

crackz report generate --project harbor_main \
  --output "Harbor_Main_Inspection_2024-11-05.docx"

docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text:
Generate reports for multiple projects: 

for project in project1 project2 project3; do
  crackz report generate --project "$project" \
    --output "reports/${project}_$(date +%Y%m%d).docx"
done

docs.title: Archive with Project
docs.text:
Keep report alongside project data: 

crackz report generate --project demo-project  # Creates demo-project/demo-project_report.docx

docs.title: Version Control
docs.text:
Track report parameters in project config: 

# Add to project notes
project:
  notes: "Report generated 2024-11-05 with default thresholds"

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Detection Workflow - Running crack detection
  • Configuration - Adjusting detection parameters
  • CLI Cookbook - Common workflow examples
  • Project Layout - Understanding project layout

docs.title: Skills Policy
docs.text: This file defines how Crackz should use agent skills.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Keep repo skills sparse, project-specific, and high-signal. Do not use the repository as a dumping ground for generic skills that are equally useful in unrelated codebases.

docs.title: Repo-Level Skills
docs.text:
A skill belongs in .agents/skills only if at least one of these is true:

  • it encodes Crackz-specific workflows or conventions
  • it reflects a recurring role in this repository
  • it reduces repeated reading of Crackz-specific docs or architecture
  • it improves consistency across Codex, Copilot, and Claude for this repository

Current preferred Crackz repo skills:

  • crackz
  • crackz-developer
  • crackz-reviewer
  • crackz-docs-writer
  • crackz-docker-specialist
  • crackz-pytorch-expert

docs.title: User-Level Skills
docs.text:
Keep these outside the repository:

  • generic Python skills
  • generic DevOps or Git skills
  • personal workflow helpers
  • plugin-provided skills
  • auth, permissions, or machine-specific behavior

These belong in user scope such as ~/.copilot/skills, ~/.codex/skills, or tool-specific plugin systems.

docs.title: Design Rules
docs.text:
• Prefer a few strong skills over many narrow ones.
  • Default to one repository-wide entry skill plus a small number of role skills.
  • Keep SKILL.md concise and point to shared docs instead of duplicating large guidance blocks.
  • Reuse docs/agent-playbook.md as the main shared reference.
  • If a skill would make sense in many repos, it probably should not live in Crackz.

docs.title: Update Rules
docs.text:
When adding a repo skill:

  1. Confirm the behavior is Crackz-specific.
  2. Keep the description explicit enough to trigger only for matching tasks.
  3. Keep the body short and point to the playbook or focused docs.
  4. Avoid overlapping heavily with another Crackz skill unless one is intentionally broader.

When removing a repo skill:

  1. Prefer removing generic skills before removing Crackz-specific ones.
  2. Verify the behavior still exists through user-level or plugin-level skills if it is still needed.

docs.title: Default Recommendation
docs.text:
For Crackz, prefer:

  • one broad entry skill: crackz
  • a handful of role skills for implementation, review, docs, Docker, and ML

Avoid maintaining a large in-repo taxonomy of generic engineering skills.

docs.title: Tracing with OpenTelemetry
docs.text: Crackz supports distributed tracing for AI operations using OpenTelemetry. This enables monitoring, debugging, and performance analysis of AI model calls and workflows.

docs.title: 1. Install Tracing Dependencies
docs.text:
uv sync --extra tracing

This installs: - opentelemetry-instrumentation-anthropic - Instruments Anthropic SDK - opentelemetry-sdk - OpenTelemetry core SDK - opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http - OTLP HTTP exporter

docs.title: 2. Start AI Toolkit Trace Collector
docs.text:
In VS Code, run command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P):

AI Toolkit: Open Tracing

Or use command ID: ai-mlstudio.tracing.open

This starts the local trace collector and opens the trace viewer.

docs.title: 3. Enable Tracing
docs.text:
Option A: Environment Variable (Recommended)

export CRACKZ_TRACING_ENABLED=1
crackz-gui  # Tracing auto-enabled

Option B: Programmatic

from crackz.tracing import setup_tracing

# Initialize with default AI Toolkit endpoint
setup_tracing()

# Or custom endpoint
setup_tracing(
    endpoint="http://custom-collector:4318/v1/traces",
    service_name="crackz-production"
)

docs.title: 4. View Traces
docs.text: Traces appear automatically in the AI Toolkit trace viewer. Each AI operation creates spans showing: - Request/response payloads - Latency and timing - Token usage - Errors and exceptions

docs.title: What Gets Traced
docs.text: When tracing is enabled, the following operations are automatically instrumented:

docs.title: Anthropic API Calls (AI Chat)
docs.text:
• Message creation requests
  • Streaming responses
  • Token counts
  • Model selection
  • Error conditions

Example trace: 

crackz
└── anthropic.messages.create
    ├── model: claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929
    ├── input_tokens: 1245
    ├── output_tokens: 382
    └── duration: 2.3s

docs.title: Future: PyTorch Lightning Training
docs.text:
• Training epochs
  • Validation loops
  • Checkpoint saves
  • Data loading

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Variable Default Description CRACKZ_TRACING_ENABLED 0 Enable/disable tracing (1/0)

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
AI Toolkit (Default): - HTTP: http://localhost:4318/v1/traces - gRPC: http://localhost:4317 (not used by default)

Custom Collector: 

setup_tracing(endpoint="http://your-collector:4318/v1/traces")

docs.title: CLI with Tracing
docs.text:
# Enable tracing for all CLI operations
export CRACKZ_TRACING_ENABLED=1
crackz detect run --project my_project

# Disable for specific run
export CRACKZ_TRACING_ENABLED=0
crackz detect run --project my_project

docs.title: GUI with Tracing
docs.text:
# In main.py or startup script
from crackz.tracing import setup_tracing

# Enable before starting GUI
if os.getenv("CRACKZ_TRACING_ENABLED") == "1":
    setup_tracing()

# Run GUI
from crackz_gui.qt.app import main
main()

docs.title: Programmatic API
docs.text:
from crackz.tracing import setup_tracing, shutdown_tracing

# Initialize tracing
setup_tracing(service_name="crackz-batch-processor")

# Your AI operations (automatically traced)
from crackz_gui.services.ai_chat import AIChatService
chat = AIChatService(...)
chat.send_message("Analyze this crack detection result")

# Clean shutdown (flushes pending spans)
shutdown_tracing()

docs.title: "Tracing dependencies not installed"
docs.text:
Solution: 

uv sync --extra tracing

docs.title: "Connection refused to localhost:4318"
docs.text:
Cause: AI Toolkit trace collector not running

Solution: Open trace viewer in VS Code: 

Ctrl+Shift+P → AI Toolkit: Open Tracing

docs.title: No traces appearing
docs.text: Checklist: 1. ✅ Tracing dependencies installed (uv sync --extra tracing) 2. ✅ AI Toolkit trace collector running 3. ✅ CRACKZ_TRACING_ENABLED=1 set 4. ✅ Application restarted after enabling 5. ✅ Check logs for "OpenTelemetry tracing initialized" message

docs.title: Spans missing or incomplete
docs.text:
Cause: Application crashed or didn't shut down cleanly

Solution: Call shutdown_tracing() before exit: 

import atexit
from crackz.tracing import shutdown_tracing

atexit.register(shutdown_tracing)

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text:
Tracing has minimal overhead: - Span creation: ~0.1ms per operation - Memory: ~2MB for span buffering - Network: Async batch export (default 5s intervals)

Recommendation: Enable in development/staging, optional in production.

docs.title: Integration with AI Toolkit
docs.text:
AI Toolkit provides: - Local trace collector - No external dependencies - Visual trace viewer - Interactive span timeline - Filtering and search - Find specific operations - Export capabilities - Save traces for analysis

Workflow: 1. Write code with AI operations 2. Enable tracing (CRACKZ_TRACING_ENABLED=1) 3. Run application 4. View traces in AI Toolkit panel 5. Analyze performance and behavior

docs.title: Custom Span Attributes
docs.text:
from opentelemetry import trace

tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

with tracer.start_as_current_span("custom-operation") as span:
    span.set_attribute("project.name", "harbor_alpha")
    span.set_attribute("image.count", 1024)
    # Your code here

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
By default, all spans are exported. For high-volume scenarios:

from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.sampling import TraceIdRatioBased

# Sample 10% of traces
sampler = TraceIdRatioBased(0.1)

# Pass to setup_tracing (requires custom implementation)

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry Python Docs
  • Anthropic Instrumentation
  • AI Toolkit Documentation
  • Crackz AI Chat Guide

docs.title: Support
docs.text:
• Tracing issues: Check AI Toolkit trace viewer logs
  • Crackz issues: GitHub Issues
  • OpenTelemetry issues: OpenTelemetry GitHub

docs.title: TrainingConfig Contract
docs.text:
TrainingConfig defines the core knobs for model training. It lives in crackz.project.config and is embedded under ai.training in a project.

Field Type Default Description batch_size int 8 Samples per optimizer step. num_workers int 4 DataLoader worker processes. epochs int 10 Total training epochs. learning_rate float 1e-3 Optimizer base LR. shuffle bool True Shuffle training dataset each epoch. loss str | None None Optional explicit loss override (framework default if None). metrics str | None None Optional metrics spec string. seed int | None None Global seed for reproducibility (torch, numpy, random). precision int | str | None None Mixed precision mode (16, "16-mixed", "bf16-mixed", etc.). devices int | None None Number of accelerator devices (e.g. GPUs) to use. strategy str | None None PyTorch Lightning strategy (e.g. "ddp", "ddp_spawn"). tensorboard bool False Enable TensorBoard logging to artifacts/training/tensorboard.

docs.title: Snapshot Test
docs.text:
A snapshot test (tests/unit/crackz/project/test_training_config_schema.py) guards against accidental field drift. If you intentionally change TrainingConfig:

  1. Update this document.
  2. Run the tests to see the snapshot failure.
  3. Update the snapshot (e.g. regenerate expected structure) per test instructions.
  4. Bump CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION and add a migration step if persisted YAML needs changes.

docs.title: Adding Fields Safely
docs.text:
1. Add the field with a sensible default.
  2. Update migration logic to inject the new default for legacy projects.
  3. Document the field here.
  4. Consider whether CLI flags are warranted for runtime overrides.

docs.title: Runtime Overrides
docs.text:
CLI training overrides currently support --epochs and --batch-size. Runtime changes are not persisted: they affect only the active training invocation.

To add a new override: - Extend CLI option definitions. - Apply the override after project load and (if needed) after migration.

docs.title: TensorBoard
docs.text: When tensorboard=True, logs are written under <project>/artifacts/training/tensorboard. The directory is created lazily.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Setting seed triggers seeding helper logic that affects random, NumPy, and PyTorch to the extent supported by selected device / strategy.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: A comprehensive guide to using Crackz for AI-powered crack detection and infrastructure inspection.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
Crackz is an AI-driven image analysis tool designed for detecting cracks in harbor infrastructure, bridges, and industrial facilities. It provides:

  • Automated crack detection using deep learning segmentation models
  • Flexible workflows via CLI and GUI interfaces
  • Structured project management with train/val/test/raw data splits
  • Reproducible results through configuration snapshots
  • Scalable deployment options (local, Docker, Azure Batch)
  • Open architecture supporting multiple model types and encoders

docs.title: Model Capabilities
docs.text:
Segmentation Models (Default) - Binary segmentation: Pixel-level crack/no-crack or deviation/no-deviation mapping - Multi-class segmentation: Detect multiple defect types (cracks, corrosion, spalling) - Encoder flexibility: Choose from 20+ backbones (ResNet, EfficientNet, MobileNet, etc.) - Transfer learning: Leverage ImageNet pre-trained weights or train from scratch

Classification Models (Future Extension) - Whole-image analysis: Quick assessment ("has crack" vs "no crack") - Triage workflows: Filter large image sets before detailed segmentation - Edge deployment: Lightweight models for mobile devices

docs.title: Two Deployment Paths
docs.text:
Path 1: Train Custom Model - Import labeled training data (images with ground truth masks) - Configure model architecture and hyperparameters - Train model via crackz detect train - Best for: Domain-specific data, unique defect types, custom requirements

Path 2: Use Pre-Trained Model - Acquire ready-made checkpoint from model providers or previous projects - Place checkpoint in project artifacts directory - Run detection immediately with crackz detect run - Best for: Quick deployment, standard use cases, proof-of-concept, multi-site consistency

docs.title: High-Level Workflow
docs.text:
graph LR
    A[Create Project] --> B[Import Images]
    B --> C{Need Custom Model?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Train Model]
    C -->|No| E[Run Detection]
    D --> E
    E --> F[View Results]
    F --> G{Satisfied?}
    G -->|No| H[Adjust Config]
    H --> D
    G -->|Yes| I[Export/Package]

Typical Timeline: - Initial setup: 5-10 minutes - Training (light): 5-30 minutes depending on dataset size and hardware - Detection: Seconds to minutes per image - Full workflow (first run): 30-60 minutes

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 – 3.13 (64-bit)
  • Operating System: Linux, macOS, or Windows 10/11
  • Disk Space: ~2-3 GB for PyTorch and model weights

docs.title: Optional
docs.text:
• NVIDIA GPU: CUDA-capable GPU with 4+ GB VRAM for accelerated training/detection
  • Docker: For containerized deployments

docs.title: GPU Considerations
docs.text:
Task CPU Performance GPU Benefit Detection (single image) 2-5 seconds 10-50x faster Training (small dataset, 10 epochs) 20-60 minutes 5-20x faster Batch detection (100 images) Minutes to hours Highly recommended

GPU Driver Requirements: - CUDA 11.8 or 12.1+ recommended - Driver version 520+ for CUDA 12.x - Verify: nvidia-smi should show your GPU

docs.title: 3. Installation
docs.text: See the detailed Installation guide for complete instructions. Quick reference:

docs.title: Standard CPU Install
docs.text:
# Install from GitHub Release (replace VERSION with actual version)
pip install https://github.com/Anaxiatech-AB/crackz/releases/download/vVERSION/crackz-VERSION-py3-none-any.whl

# Or download first, then install
wget https://github.com/Anaxiatech-AB/crackz/releases/download/v0.30.2/crackz-0.30.2-py3-none-any.whl
pip install crackz-0.30.2-py3-none-any.whl

# Verify installation
crackz --help

docs.title: GPU Install
docs.text:
# Install PyTorch with CUDA support first
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121

# Then install Crackz from GitHub Release
pip install https://github.com/Anaxiatech-AB/crackz/releases/download/vVERSION/crackz-VERSION-py3-none-any.whl

docs.title: Docker (No Python Required)
docs.text:
# CPU version
docker pull ghcr.io/anaxiatech-ab/crackz:latest

# GPU version (requires nvidia-docker)
docker pull ghcr.io/anaxiatech-ab/crackz:gpu

# Slim version (minimal runtime)
docker pull ghcr.io/anaxiatech-ab/crackz:slim

Registry URL: https://github.com/Anaxiatech-AB?tab=packages&repo_name=crackz

Verify Installation: 

crackz --version
python -c "import crackz; print('Crackz installed successfully')"

docs.title: 4. Quick Start
docs.text: Complete end-to-end workflow in under 10 minutes:

docs.title: Step 1: Initialize a Project
docs.text:
crackz init --name my-first-project
cd my-first-project

This creates the following structure: 

my-first-project/
├── images/          # Image storage by split
│   ├── raw/         # Unprocessed images for inference
│   ├── train/       # Training images
│   ├── val/         # Validation images
│   └── test/        # Test images
├── masks/           # Ground truth masks (optional for raw)
│   ├── train/
│   ├── val/
│   └── test/
├── artifacts/       # Model outputs (metrics, plots)
├── detections/      # Detection results (annotated images, JSON)
├── models/          # Saved model weights (or checkpoints/ in older projects)
├── logs/            # Project-specific logs
└── project.yaml     # Project configuration

Note: Older projects may use checkpoints/ instead of models/. Use crackz migrate --project <project> --migrate-files to upgrade to the new structure, or the GUI will prompt you automatically when opening the project.

docs.title: Step 2: Import Images
docs.text:
# Import sample images for detection (no training)
crackz import-images \
  --project my-first-project \
  --src ./samples \
  --type raw \
  --size 512 512

What happens: - Images resized to 512×512 pixels (preserving aspect ratio with padding) - Normalized and validated - Copied to images/raw/

docs.title: Step 3: Run Detection (Lite Mode)
docs.text:
# Use pre-trained model
crackz detect run --project my-first-project

Results appear in: - detections/ - Annotated images with highlighted cracks - artifacts/metrics.json - Detection statistics

docs.title: Step 4: (Optional) Train on Custom Data
docs.text:
If you have labeled training data: 

# Import training images with masks
crackz import-images \
  --project my-first-project \
  --src ./training-data/images \
  --src-masks ./training-data/masks \
  --type train \
  --size 512 512

# Quick training (1 epoch for testing)
crackz detect train --project my-first-project --epochs 1 --batch-size 2

docs.title: Step 5: View Results
docs.text:
Command Line: 

# Check detection outputs
ls my-first-project/detections/

# View metrics
cat my-first-project/artifacts/metrics.json

# Open annotated images
open my-first-project/detections/*.png  # macOS
xdg-open my-first-project/detections/*.png  # Linux

Interactive Dashboard: 

# Launch Streamlit dashboard for advanced analysis
crackz dashboard --project my-first-project

GUI Integration: 

# Open project in GUI and launch dashboard
crackz-gui
# Then: Tools → Launch Dashboard

The interactive dashboard provides advanced visualization features: - Detection result gallery with filtering and sorting - Training metrics visualization with loss curves and performance charts - GPS mapping for geotagged images showing crack locations - Parameter tuning interface for threshold adjustment - Export capabilities for reports and analysis

For detailed dashboard features, see the Dashboard Guide.

docs.title: 5.1 Project Layout
docs.text: Project Directory Structure: - images/: Organized by split (raw/train/val/test) - Use raw/ for inference-only images - Use train/val/test/ for model development - masks/: Ground truth segmentation masks (required for train/val/test) - Must match image filenames exactly - Binary masks: 0 = background, 255 = crack - artifacts/: Training outputs (loss curves, metrics JSON) - detections/: Detection results with overlays - models/: Saved model weights (.ckpt files) [or checkpoints/ in older projects] - logs/: Project-specific log files - project.yaml: Configuration file (version-controlled)

docs.title: 5.2 Data Splits Explained
docs.text:
Split Purpose Masks Required? When to Use raw Production inference No Real-world images for detection train Model training Yes Learning crack patterns val Hyperparameter tuning Yes Model selection, early stopping test Final evaluation Yes Unbiased performance report

Best Practices: - Never tune on test data (use validation instead) - Typical split ratios: 70% train, 15% val, 15% test - Minimum validation set: 10-20 images - Keep test set untouched until final evaluation

docs.title: 5.3 Artifacts
docs.text:
Generated outputs from training and detection:

Training Artifacts: - metrics.json - Per-epoch loss, IoU, F1 scores - loss_curve.png - Training/validation loss visualization - confusion_matrix.png - Classification performance (if applicable)

Detection Artifacts: - Annotated images in detections/ with crack overlays - metrics.json - Summary statistics (total cracks, coverage %) - Optional: Bounding box coordinates, crack area measurements

docs.title: 5.4 Logging Model
docs.text:
Crackz uses a hybrid two-tier logging system:

Layer Location When Active Purpose Central System temp or CRACKZ_LOG_DIR Always Captures issues before/without project Project <project>/logs/ After project load Project-specific diagnostics

Configuration: 

# Set central log directory
export CRACKZ_LOG_DIR=~/crackz-logs

# Both central and project logs will be written
crackz detect run --project my-project

Log Levels: - --debug: Verbose output (all operations) - Default: Info level (key events only) - --quiet: Minimal output (errors only)

docs.title: 5.5 Schema Versioning
docs.text:
Projects include a schema version for forward compatibility:

schema_version: "1.0"
project:
  name: my-project
  # ... rest of config

Migrating Old Projects: 

crackz migrate --project old-project

See Migration Guide for details.

docs.title: 5.6 Model Selection & Configuration
docs.text:
Crackz supports multiple model architectures to match different use cases.

Choosing a Model Type

Use Case Model Type Configuration Precise crack mapping Binary segmentation num_classes: 1 (default) Multiple defect types Multi-class segmentation num_classes: 3 (e.g., crack/corrosion/spalling) Quick screening Classification (future) Custom model class

Encoder Selection

The encoder is the backbone network that extracts features from images. EfficientNet models are recommended for crack detection due to superior fine-grained pattern recognition:

Encoder Speed Accuracy Memory Use Case efficientnet-b3 Medium Excellent Medium ⭐ Recommended - Best for crack detection efficientnet-b0 Medium Excellent Low Budget-friendly, still excellent resnet34 Medium Very Good Medium Default - solid baseline efficientnet-b7 Slow Best High Maximum accuracy, resource-intensive resnet50 Slow Very Good High Large datasets, ResNet alternative resnet101 Very Slow Very Good Very High Research, very large datasets mobilenet_v2 Fast Fair Low Edge deployment, real-time resnet18 Fast Good Low Rapid prototyping densenet121 Medium Very Good Medium Dense connections, good gradients

Configuration Example

Edit <project>/<project>_project.yaml:

ai:
  model:
    encoder: resnet34           # Choose encoder backbone
    encoder_weights: imagenet   # Use transfer learning (recommended)
    in_channels: 3              # RGB images (use 1 for grayscale)
    num_classes: 1              # Binary segmentation
    threshold: 0.5              # Detection sensitivity (0.3=more sensitive, 0.7=less)

  training:
    epochs: 20                  # Number of training iterations
    batch_size: 8               # Images per batch (reduce if out of memory)
    learning_rate: 0.001        # Optimizer learning rate

Pre-Trained vs Custom Training

Scenario Recommendation Checkpoint Source Standard concrete cracks Use pre-trained Acquire from model provider Harbor-specific patterns Train custom Import labeled harbor images Bridge multi-defect Pre-trained or fine-tune Start with general model, adapt Proof-of-concept Use pre-trained Quick deployment Production deployment Train custom Domain-specific data

Acquiring Pre-Trained Models

Pre-trained checkpoints can come from: 1. Model providers: Commercial or open-source model repositories 2. Previous projects: Reuse successful models across sites 3. Partners: Share validated models within organization 4. Transfer learning: Fine-tune from general-purpose checkpoint

Importing Models:

Use the model import command to add a pre-trained model to your project:

crackz model import --project ./my_project --model pretrained_model.zip

Or use the GUI: 1. Right-click on the models folder (or checkpoints in older projects) 2. Select "📥 Import Model..." 3. Choose a model package file

Exporting Models:

Share or backup your trained models:

crackz model export --project ./my_project --out my_model.zip

Or use the GUI: 1. Right-click on the models folder (or checkpoints in older projects) 2. Select "📦 Export Model..." 3. Choose where to save the package

Model packages are portable zip files containing the checkpoint and metadata, making it easy to transfer models between projects, team members, or deployment environments.

Switching Encoders Mid-Project

To change encoder on an existing project: 1. Edit project.yaml → ai.model.encoder 2. Re-train the model: crackz detect train --project <name> 3. New checkpoint will use updated encoder

See Configuration Reference for complete model configuration options.

docs.title: 6.1 Create a New Project
docs.text:
CLI: 

crackz init --name harbor-inspection-2025 --description "Q1 2025 harbor crack survey"

GUI: 1. Launch: crackz-gui 2. File → New Project (Cmd/Ctrl+N) 3. Select base folder and enter project name 4. Project structure created automatically

Advanced Options: 

# Create with custom settings
crackz init --name custom-project --force  # Overwrite if exists

# Initialize from template (future)
crackz init --name new-project --template harbor-config.yaml

docs.title: 6.2 Import Images
docs.text:
From Local Directory: 

crackz import-images \
  --project harbor-inspection-2025 \
  --src ~/Pictures/harbor-photos \
  --type raw \
  --size 512 512

With Ground Truth Masks: 

crackz import-images \
  --project harbor-inspection-2025 \
  --src ~/labeled-data/images \
  --src-masks ~/labeled-data/masks \
  --type train \
  --size 512 512

Batch Import Multiple Splits: 

# Training data
crackz import-images --project my-project --src train_imgs --src-masks train_masks --type train --size 512 512

# Validation data
crackz import-images --project my-project --src val_imgs --src-masks val_masks --type val --size 512 512

# Test data
crackz import-images --project my-project --src test_imgs --src-masks test_masks --type test --size 512 512

Supported Formats: - Images: .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .bmp, .tif, .tiff - Masks: .png (grayscale, 0=background, 255=crack)

Image Preprocessing: - Resizing with aspect ratio preservation - Zero-padding to target size - Normalization (mean/std from ImageNet)

docs.title: 6.2.1 Creating Masks Manually
docs.text: If you don't have pre-labeled masks, you can create them using the Crackz mask editor in the GUI:

docs.title: Quick Start: Creating Your First Mask
docs.text:
1. Open the GUI and Your Project 

crackz-gui
Then open your project via File → Open Project.

2. Navigate to Images - In the project browser tree, expand images/train/ (or any split) - You'll see your imported images in the thumbnail view

3. Open Mask Editor Choose one of three methods: - Right-click an image → 🎨 Edit Mask - Click the 🎨 badge below the image thumbnail - Click the image to preview, then click 🎨 Edit Mask button

4. Paint Your Mask - Click 🖌️ Brush tool (or press B) - Adjust Brush Size slider (start with 30-50px for large cracks) - Paint over crack areas—watch the green circle cursor show your brush size - Use 🧹 Eraser (or press E) to fix mistakes - Use ↶ Undo (Ctrl+Z) if needed—you have 20 undo levels

5. Save and Continue - Click 💾 Save Mask when done - The mask is automatically saved to masks/train/ with the same filename - Repeat for more images

Typical annotation time: 30 seconds to 3 minutes per image, depending on crack complexity.

docs.title: Mask Editor Features
docs.text:
The mask editor is a professional-grade annotation tool with:

  • Two-row toolbar: All tools visible without crowding
  • Visual brush cursor: Green circle shows brush size, red for eraser
  • Undo/Redo: 20 levels of history for safe editing
  • Clear button: Reset the entire mask with one click (with confirmation)
  • Opacity adjustment: See through the mask to verify alignment
  • Keyboard shortcuts: B for brush, E for eraser, Ctrl+Z to undo

For detailed UI reference, see the GUI Guide: Mask Editor section.

docs.title: Best Practices for Manual Annotation
docs.text:
Quality Guidelines: - ✅ Cover cracks fully: Paint the entire crack width, not just the centerline - ✅ Include fine details: Don't skip hairline cracks—they help training - ✅ Consistent labeling: Use the same criteria across all images (e.g., always include crack shadows) - ✅ Check at low opacity: Lower opacity to 0.2-0.3 to verify you didn't miss anything - ❌ Don't over-paint: Only paint actual cracks, not stains or texture variations - ❌ Don't rush: Quality > quantity—a few good masks beat many poor ones

Efficiency Tips: - Start with large brush (50-100px) for quick coverage of wide cracks - Switch to small brush (5-20px) for fine details and edges - Use keyboard shortcuts (B, E, Ctrl+Z) instead of clicking buttons - Save frequently: Don't lose work—save after each image - Take breaks: Annotation fatigue reduces quality after ~30 minutes

Annotation Order: 1. Annotate diverse examples first: Cover different crack types, locations, and lighting conditions 2. Aim for 30-50 images minimum before first training run 3. Then use semi-automated workflows: See Phase 2B: Semi-Automated Mask Creation

docs.title: How Many Masks Do You Need?
docs.text:
Dataset Size Use Case Recommendation 10-30 masks Proof-of-concept Sufficient for initial testing, not production 50-100 masks Small project Good starting point for custom training 100-500 masks Standard project Recommended for reliable production model 500-2000 masks Large project Ideal for high-accuracy, generalized model 2000+ masks Research/enterprise Maximizes robustness and edge case handling

Note: With mask propagation (Phase 2B), you can manually annotate ~50 images and semi-automatically create 100-500+ masks, dramatically reducing effort.

Next Step: After creating masks, proceed to 6.3 Train a Model.

docs.title: 6.3 Train a Model
docs.text:
Basic Training: 

crackz detect train --project my-project

With Runtime Overrides: 

crackz detect train \
  --project my-project \
  --epochs 20 \
  --batch-size 8 \
  --learning-rate 0.001

Note: Runtime overrides are not saved to project.yaml - they're for experimentation only.

GPU Training: 

# Automatically uses GPU if available
crackz detect train --project my-project --epochs 50

# Verify GPU is being used (check logs)
tail -f my-project/logs/crackz.log | grep -i cuda

Monitor Training Progress: 

# Watch loss in real-time
tail -f my-project/artifacts/metrics.json

# Or use TensorBoard (if enabled)
tensorboard --logdir my-project/artifacts/tensorboard

Early Stopping: Training automatically stops if validation loss doesn't improve for 5 epochs (configurable in project.yaml).

docs.title: 6.4 Run Detection
docs.text:
CPU Detection: 

crackz detect run --project my-project

GPU Detection: 

# Uses GPU automatically if available
crackz detect run --project my-project

# Force CPU (even with GPU available)
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" crackz detect run --project my-project

Model Selection:

By default, detection automatically selects the best available checkpoint. You can override this with the --model option:

# Auto-select (default): best.ckpt > last.ckpt > final.ckpt
crackz detect run --project my-project

# Explicitly use best checkpoint
crackz detect run --project my-project --model best

# Use most recent checkpoint (useful during iterative development)
crackz detect run --project my-project --model last

# Use final checkpoint
crackz detect run --project my-project --model final

# Use specific epoch checkpoint (e.g., epoch-0.9234.ckpt)
crackz detect run --project my-project --model epoch-0.9234

Checkpoint Priority (Auto-selection): 1. best.ckpt - Highest validation IoU during training (recommended for production) 2. last.ckpt - Most recent training checkpoint 3. final.ckpt - Final training checkpoint

When to Use Each: - Auto-select (no --model flag): Standard production inference - --model best: Explicitly ensure highest-performing model is used - --model last: Test most recent training state during development - --model final: Use final training state (may differ from best if validation IoU decreased) - --model epoch-X: Compare performance across different epochs or reproduce specific results

Example: Compare Models: 

# Run detection with different checkpoints to compare results
crackz detect run --project my-project --model best
mv my-project/detections my-project/detections-best

crackz detect run --project my-project --model last
mv my-project/detections my-project/detections-last

crackz detect run --project my-project --model epoch-0.8532
mv my-project/detections my-project/detections-epoch-0.8532

# Compare detection outputs side by side

Detection on Specific Split: 

# Detect on raw images (default)
crackz detect run --project my-project

# Detect on test set (with metrics if masks available)
crackz detect run --project my-project --split test

Batch Processing: 

# Process multiple projects
for project in project1 project2 project3; do
    crackz detect run --project $project
done

Docker Detection: 

# CPU
docker run --rm \
  -v $(pwd)/my-project:/home/app/my-project \
  ghcr.io/anaxiatech-ab/crackz-cli:latest \
  detect run --project /home/app/my-project

# GPU
docker run --gpus all --rm \
  -v $(pwd)/my-project:/home/app/my-project \
  ghcr.io/anaxiatech-ab/crackz-cli:gpu \
  detect run --project /home/app/my-project

docs.title: 6.5 View Metrics (TensorBoard)
docs.text:
Enable TensorBoard in Configuration:

Edit project.yaml: 

training:
  tensorboard: true

Or create a config override: 

# tensorboard-config.yaml
training:
  tensorboard: true

Start TensorBoard: 

# After training with tensorboard enabled
tensorboard --logdir my-project/artifacts/tensorboard

# Open browser to http://localhost:6006

What You'll See: - Loss curves (training & validation) - IoU metrics over epochs - Learning rate schedule - Sample predictions (if configured)

Alternative: View JSON Metrics 

# Quick summary
cat my-project/artifacts/metrics.json | python -m json.tool

# Extract specific metrics
cat my-project/artifacts/metrics.json | jq '.final_val_iou'

See Configuration Reference - TensorBoard Integration for details.

docs.title: 6.6 Clean and Maintain Projects
docs.text:
Preview Cleanup: 

crackz clean --project my-project --dry-run

Clean Logs and Artifacts: 

crackz clean --project my-project

Clean Logs Only: 

crackz clean --project my-project --logs-only

What Gets Removed: - *.log files - Temporary training artifacts - Old checkpoint files (keeps best/last) - Detection outputs (optional)

Checkpoint Pruning:

Keep only the best N checkpoints (configured in project.yaml): 

training:
  checkpoint:
    save_top_k: 3  # Keep top 3 checkpoints by validation loss

Manual pruning: 

# Remove all but the last checkpoint
rm my-project/checkpoints/*.ckpt
# (except last-*.ckpt)

# Or keep only best checkpoint
rm my-project/checkpoints/epoch*.ckpt
# (keep best-*.ckpt)

docs.title: 6.7 Phase 2: Semi-Automated Mask Creation
docs.text:
Phase 2 introduces AI-assisted workflows to accelerate annotation and reduce manual labeling effort by 50-80%. These features are available in the GUI and (partially) via CLI.

📘 For comprehensive GUI workflow documentation, see GUI Guide: Phase 2B Semi-Automated Workflows.

This section covers CLI-based workflows for automation and scripting.

docs.title: Active Learning Workflow (CLI)
docs.text:
Use uncertainty-based prioritization to maximize annotation efficiency:

Step 1: Train initial model on small labeled dataset 

# Train on 50-100 manually labeled images
crackz detect train --project harbor-project --epochs 10

Step 2: Find most uncertain images 

# Prioritize top 50 images from raw/unlabeled pool
uv run crackz active-learning run \
  --project harbor-project \
  --split raw \
  --top-n 50 \
  --method entropy \
  --out priorities.json

Available uncertainty methods: - entropy - High entropy = uncertain predictions (default) - max_probability - Low confidence = needs review - variance - High disagreement across pixels - mean_confidence - Distance from decision boundary

Step 3: Annotate prioritized images 

# Use GUI mask editor or external tools
# Focus on top-ranked images from priorities.json

Step 4: Import new annotations and retrain 

# Move annotated images to train split
crackz import-images --project harbor-project \
  --src annotated_batch \
  --src-masks annotated_masks \
  --type train

# Retrain with expanded dataset
crackz detect train --project harbor-project --epochs 15

Step 5: Repeat cycle Continue active learning iterations until desired accuracy.

docs.title: Mask Propagation Workflow (CLI)
docs.text:
For GUI-based mask propagation with visual similarity tuning, see GUI Guide: Mask Propagation Workflow.

This section covers CLI-based propagation for automation and batch processing.

Copy masks across similar images using feature matching:

Step 1: Manually annotate reference image Create high-quality mask for one representative image (e.g., wall_section_01.jpg).

Step 2: Find similar images 

# Preview similarity scores
uv run crackz propagate-masks find-similar \
  --project harbor-project \
  --reference wall_section_01.jpg \
  --split raw \
  --out similarities.json

Step 3: Propagate mask 

# Copy mask to similar images (>80% similarity)
uv run crackz propagate-masks run \
  --project harbor-project \
  --reference wall_section_01.jpg \
  --mask wall_section_01_mask.png \
  --split raw \
  --threshold 0.8 \
  --out propagated_masks/

Step 4: Review and correct 

# Import propagated masks
crackz import-images --project harbor-project \
  --src images_with_propagated \
  --src-masks propagated_masks \
  --type train

# Review in GUI mask editor - correct errors before training

When to use mask propagation: - Same structure from different angles (e.g., harbor wall sections) - Sequential video frames (drone walkthrough) - Temporal monitoring (same location over time) - Adjacent sections of continuous structures

Parameter tuning: 

# More permissive (more propagations, less reliable)
--threshold 0.6 --min-matches 5

# Stricter (fewer propagations, higher quality)
--threshold 0.9 --min-matches 20 --sift

Output: Propagated masks include confidence scores for quality assessment.

docs.title: Combined Workflow: Active Learning + Propagation
docs.text:
Step 1: Initial training (50 manual annotations) 

crackz detect train --project harbor-project

Step 2: Find uncertain images 

uv run crackz active-learning run \
  --project harbor-project \
  --top-n 20 \
  --method entropy \
  --out uncertain.json

Step 3: Manually annotate 5 diverse reference images Select images covering different viewpoints/structures from uncertain.json.

Step 4: Propagate masks 

# For each reference image
uv run crackz propagate-masks run \
  --reference ref1.jpg --mask ref1_mask.png \
  --project harbor-project --threshold 0.8

# Propagate remaining references...

Step 5: Review + import + retrain 

# Import all propagated masks
crackz import-images --project harbor-project \
  --src propagated_images \
  --src-masks propagated_masks \
  --type train

# Retrain with 50 original + ~40 propagated = 90 annotations
crackz detect train --project harbor-project --epochs 15

Step 6: Repeat active learning cycle Continue until target accuracy (e.g., IoU >0.85).

Efficiency gains: - Traditional: 200 manual annotations (~40 hours) - With Phase 2: 60 manual + 140 propagated (~15 hours) - 60% time reduction for equivalent model performance

docs.title: 6.7 Package or Distribute
docs.text:
Export Unified Configuration: 

crackz export-config \
  --project my-project \

Share Project:

tar -czf my-project.tar.gz \
  --exclude='checkpoints' \
  --exclude='detections' \

# Send to collaborator

Create PowerShell Alias:

Or:

docs.text:

Key Features: - Project Browser: Navigate project structure with folder tree - Image Preview: Thumbnail grid for image directories - Text Preview: Syntax-highlighted JSON/YAML/Markdown viewer - Double-click Images: Opens full-size popup - Context Menu: Right-click for quick actions (import, clean, open in explorer)

docs.title: 10.1 Installation Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Installation fails with dependency errors

Solution: 

# Update pip and setuptools
pip install --upgrade pip setuptools

# Download and install from GitHub Release
wget https://github.com/Anaxiatech-AB/crackz/releases/download/vVERSION/crackz-VERSION-py3-none-any.whl
pip install crackz-VERSION-py3-none-any.whl

Problem: CUDA not detected despite having GPU

Solution: 

# Verify CUDA installation
nvidia-smi

# Check PyTorch CUDA support
python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"

# Reinstall PyTorch with CUDA
pip uninstall torch torchvision
pip install torch torchvision --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121

docs.title: 10.2 Import/Training Issues
docs.text:
Problem: No images found in training split

Solution: - Verify images are in images/train/ (not images/raw/) - Check file extensions (.jpg, .jpeg, .png, .bmp, .tif, .tiff only) - Ensure import command used --type train

Problem: Training says "No masks found"

Solution: - Masks required for train/val/test splits - Check masks are in masks/train/ with same filenames as images - Masks must be grayscale PNG: 0=background, 255=crack

Problem: Out of memory during training

Solution: 

# Reduce batch size
crackz detect train --project my-project --batch-size 1

# Or reduce image size
crackz import-images --project my-project --src ./data --type train --size 256 256

# Monitor GPU memory
nvidia-smi -l 1  # Update every second

docs.title: 10.3 Detection Issues
docs.text:
Problem: Empty detections directory after running detect

Solution: - Check logs: tail my-project/logs/crackz.log - Verify images exist in target split (default: raw/) - Ensure checkpoint exists: ls my-project/models/ (or my-project/checkpoints/ in older projects) - Try: crackz detect run --project my-project --debug

Problem: Detection results look wrong (too many/few cracks)

Solution: - Adjust threshold in project.yaml: 

detection:
  threshold: 0.5  # Pixel-level binarization threshold
                  # Increase to reduce false positives (0.7)
                  # Decrease to catch more cracks (0.3)

  # Severity categorization thresholds (crack area %)
  min_confidence: 0.005     # Min to save (0.5% crack area)
  medium_confidence: 0.02   # "Probable Crack" threshold (2%)
  high_confidence: 0.05     # "Crack Detected" threshold (5%)
  min_crack_area_px: 100    # Filter out detections < 100 pixels
- Retrain model with more/better labeled data - Check that images are similar to training data

docs.title: 10.4 Logging Issues
docs.text:
Problem: No logs written

Solution: 

# Check permissions
ls -la $(python -c "import tempfile; print(tempfile.gettempdir())")/crackz_logs

# Set explicit log directory
export CRACKZ_LOG_DIR=~/crackz-logs
mkdir -p ~/crackz-logs
crackz detect run --project my-project

Problem: Central logs filling up disk

Solution: 

# Clean old logs
rm -rf $CRACKZ_LOG_DIR/*.log

# Or set retention policy (future feature)
# See configuration.md for log rotation settings

docs.title: 10.5 Common Error Messages
docs.text: Error Cause Solution Missing --project or --cfg Project not specified Add --project <name> or --cfg <file> CUDA out of memory Batch size too large Reduce --batch-size Schema version mismatch Old project format Run crackz migrate --project <name> Permission denied writing logs Insufficient permissions Check directory permissions or set CRACKZ_LOG_DIR No checkpoint found Model not trained Train first: crackz detect train --project <name>

docs.title: 11.1 Licensing
docs.text:
Q: Is Crackz free to use?

A: Crackz is commercial software with a source-available license. Contact theresia.sofia.snow@gmail.com for: - Commercial licenses (perpetual, per-organization) - Volume discounts for multi-site deployments - Proof-of-concept projects - Custom training and support

See License and Customer Guide for details.

Q: Can I use Crackz for academic research?

A: Academic licenses may be available. Contact the author to discuss your research project.

docs.title: 11.2 Configuration
docs.text:
Q: Where do logs go?

A: Crackz uses a hybrid logging system: - Central logs: $CRACKZ_LOG_DIR (env var) or system temp (e.g., /tmp/crackz_logs) - Project logs: <project>/logs/ (always, in addition to central)

Both log sinks are active when a project is loaded.

Q: How do I override epochs without changing project.yaml?

A: Use runtime overrides (CLI flags): 

crackz detect train --project my-project --epochs 50 --batch-size 8

These are not saved to project.yaml - for permanent changes, edit the YAML directly or use the GUI settings dialog.

Q: Can I use a custom YAML config file?

A: Yes: 

crackz detect run --cfg my-custom-config.yaml

Or export a snapshot: 

crackz export-config --project my-project --out snapshot.yaml
crackz detect run --cfg snapshot.yaml

docs.title: 11.3 Data & Models
docs.text:
Q: What image formats are supported?

A: .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .bmp, .tif, .tiff

Q: What should mask images look like?

A: Grayscale PNG files where: - 0 (black) = background - 255 (white) = crack

Masks must have the exact same filename as corresponding images.

Q: Can I use pre-trained models from other sources?

A: Crackz uses segmentation models from segmentation-models-pytorch. You can: - Use built-in encoders (ResNet, EfficientNet, etc.) - Load custom checkpoints with --checkpoint <path> - Transfer learning from ImageNet pretrained weights (default)

Q: How do I improve detection accuracy?

A: 1. Add more training data (especially hard examples) 2. Balance your dataset (similar number of cracked/non-cracked images) 3. Increase training epochs (default is often too low) 4. Adjust threshold (detection sensitivity) 5. Try different encoders (edit project.yaml → model.encoder)

docs.title: 11.4 Performance
docs.text:
Q: How can I speed up training?

A: - Use GPU (10-50x faster) - Increase --batch-size (up to GPU memory limit) - Reduce image resolution (--size 256 256 instead of 512 512) - Use a smaller encoder (e.g., mobilenet_v2 vs resnet50)

Q: Can I run multiple detections in parallel?

A: Yes, either: - Multiple Docker containers on same host - Azure Batch for distributed processing - Bash loop with & for background jobs: 

for p in project1 project2 project3; do
    crackz detect run --project $p &
done
wait

docs.title: 12. Glossary
docs.text:
Artifact: Generated output file from training or detection (metrics, plots, annotated images).

Central Log: System-wide log location (before/outside specific projects), controlled by CRACKZ_LOG_DIR.

Checkpoint: Saved model weights (.ckpt file) from a training run. Used for resuming training or running detection.

Detection: Inference process that applies a trained model to identify cracks in images.

Encoder: Backbone network of the segmentation model (e.g., ResNet, EfficientNet). Extracts features from images.

IoU (Intersection over Union): Metric measuring overlap between predicted and ground truth masks. Range: 0-1 (higher is better).

Mask: Binary image representing ground truth (training) or predicted (detection) crack locations.

Project: Self-contained directory with images, configuration, and outputs following Crackz structure.

Schema Version: Version number in project.yaml indicating config format. Used for migrations when format changes.

Split: Data subset category - one of raw, train, val, or test.

Threshold: Confidence level (0-1) for classifying pixels as crack vs. background. Lower = more sensitive.

docs.text: This page documents the Crackz codebase structure via an automated knowledge graph—built from code imports, calls, class hierarchies, and dependency analysis. Updated on every code commit.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
• Interactive graph: Open graphify-out/graph.json in Gephi or use the local Obsidian vault
  • Obsidian vault: Open graphify-out/obsidian/ as a new vault for local PKM + graph view
  • Query from CLI: graphify query "what does Project do?" (requires local graphify install)

docs.title: Key Abstractions (God Nodes)
docs.text:
These nodes have the highest connectivity—they're the architectural center:

Node Edges Role ModelRegistry 79 Model lifecycle hub—registration, loading, checkpointing QtAppState 63 GUI state management—reactive updates across views MainWindow 62 Top-level Qt container—orchestrates all panels AIChatService 57 LLM integration—chat, embedding, inference Project 46 Configuration & metadata—spans 23 communities (chokepoint)

⚠️ Architectural risk: Project, ModelRegistry, and train() span many communities. Consider refactoring to reduce coupling.

docs.title: Code Organization (561 Communities)
docs.text:
The graph detected 561 communities—clusters of tightly connected code. Top communities:

  • Community 0 (54 nodes): Annotation config, schema, image operations
  • Community 1 (33 nodes): Database layer, projects persistence
  • Community 2 (25 nodes): Training pipeline, model checkpointing
  • ... (558 more)

Most communities are well-separated (cohesion ~0.04). See graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md for the full breakdown.

docs.title: Surprising Connections
docs.text:
These edges cross community boundaries—potential refactoring opportunities:

  • CLI→GUI: _do_edit_mask() (CLI) calls MaskEditorDialog (GUI)—suggests cross-layer bleed
  • Test→Core: Tests reach deep into config, not just public APIs
  • Training→Metrics: run_training_qt() reaches into core metrics cleanup

docs.title: Explore a Concept
docs.text:
graphify query "what is ModelRegistry connected to?"
graphify explain "Project"

docs.title: Find Shortest Path
docs.text: graphify path "MainWindow" "AIChatService"

docs.title: View in Obsidian
docs.text:
1. Open graphify-out/obsidian/ as a new vault in Obsidian
  2. Enable Graph view (Ctrl/Cmd + G)
  3. Color coding by community, search for nodes

docs.title: Update After Code Changes
docs.text:
graphify --update .

(Or it updates automatically on every git commit via the post-commit hook.)

docs.title: Graph Quality
docs.text:
• Extraction method: AST + semantic analysis (code imports, calls, class hierarchy, cross-file patterns)
  • Confidence tags: EXTRACTED (definite), INFERRED (reasoned), AMBIGUOUS (uncertain)
  • Node count: 6,555
  • Edge count: 10,806
  • Cost: AST-only (no API calls, fully local)

docs.title: Architecture Decisions
docs.text:
Key technical decisions and their rationale (ADR-style)

This document records important architecture decisions made during Crackz development. Each decision includes context, the decision itself, and consequences.

docs.title: Format
docs.text: Each decision follows this structure: - Context: Why we needed to make a decision - Decision: What we chose - Consequences: Trade-offs and implications - Status: Active | Deprecated | Superseded

docs.title: ADR-001: Use uv for Dependency Management + hatchling for Builds
docs.text:
Context: Python package management is slow with pip and complex with poetry. Additionally, setuptools as a build backend is aging and lacks modern features.

Decision: Use a hybrid approach: - uv (Astral's package manager) for dependency management, lockfiles, and task execution - hatchling (PyPA-official build backend) for building wheels and sdists

Consequences: - ✅ 10-100x faster installs compared to pip (via uv) - ✅ Automatic virtual environment management (via uv) - ✅ Built-in lockfile support via uv.lock (deterministic builds) - ✅ Modern PEP 517-compliant build backend (hatchling) - ✅ Better build defaults (uses .gitignore for sdist) - ✅ Preserves custom PyTorch index routing (uv feature) - ✅ Compatible with python-semantic-release for versioning - ⚠️ Two tools instead of one (but clear separation of concerns) - ⚠️ Relatively new toolchain (requires team adoption)

Status: Active (Updated 2025-11-30)

Related: .github/workflows/, pyproject.toml, Dockerfile*, all documentation

Migration Notes: - Migrated from setuptools to hatchling in v0.67.0 - All existing uv configuration preserved (PyTorch routing unchanged) - Semantic versioning still managed by python-semantic-release

docs.title: ADR-002: PyTorch Lightning for ML Pipeline
docs.text:
Context: Raw PyTorch requires significant boilerplate for training loops, checkpointing, and distributed training.

Decision: Use PyTorch Lightning as the ML framework layer.

Consequences: - ✅ Production-ready training with minimal boilerplate - ✅ Built-in checkpointing, logging, and callbacks - ✅ Easy GPU/multi-GPU scaling - ✅ TensorBoard integration out of the box - ⚠️ Additional abstraction layer to learn - ⚠️ Opinionated structure (less flexibility)

Status: Active

Related: core/src/crackz/ai/training.py, core/src/crackz/ai/models.py

docs.title: ADR-003: Typer for CLI Framework
docs.text:
Context: Need type-safe CLI with good DX, auto-generated help, and modern Python features.

Decision: Use Typer instead of Click or argparse.

Consequences: - ✅ Type hints drive CLI interface (DRY principle) - ✅ Excellent auto-generated help text - ✅ Easy to test and maintain - ✅ Built on Click (mature foundation) - ⚠️ Less flexible than raw Click for complex UIs - ⚠️ Learning curve for developers used to argparse

Status: Active

Related: core/src/crackz/cli/, all CLI commands

docs.title: ADR-004: CustomTkinter for GUI (Not Qt)
docs.text:
Context: Need lightweight desktop GUI. Qt requires commercial licensing for proprietary software; Tkinter is too basic.

Decision: Use CustomTkinter (modern Tkinter wrapper) instead of Qt or Kivy.

Consequences: - ✅ No licensing costs (compatible with GPL-3.0) - ✅ Modern dark mode support - ✅ Lightweight (~1MB vs Qt's ~50MB) - ✅ Easy to package with PyInstaller - ⚠️ Less feature-rich than Qt - ⚠️ Limited third-party widgets - ⚠️ Known issue: some customers want Qt migration (#127)

Status: Active (Qt migration under consideration)

Related: gui/src/crackz_gui/, issue #127

docs.title: ADR-005: Pydantic v2 for Configuration
docs.text:
Context: Need type-safe config validation with YAML serialization. Manual validation is error-prone.

Decision: Use Pydantic v2 models for all configuration with YAML backend.

Consequences: - ✅ Type-safe validation at load time - ✅ Auto-generated JSON schemas - ✅ Excellent error messages for invalid configs - ✅ Easy to extend and version (schema_version field) - ⚠️ YAML library dependency (pyyaml) - ⚠️ Learning curve for Pydantic's API

Status: Active

Related: core/src/crackz/config/, project YAML files

docs.title: ADR-006: Hybrid Logging Architecture
docs.text:
Context: Need system-wide logs for debugging AND per-project logs for customer audit trails.

Decision: Implement hybrid logging with: - Central log sink (pre-project operations, global context) - Per-project log sink (project-specific operations)

Consequences: - ✅ Complete audit trail per project - ✅ System-wide logging for debugging - ✅ Flexible central log location (env var, flag, or temp) - ⚠️ Slightly more complex logging setup - ⚠️ Two log locations to manage

Status: Active

Related: core/src/crackz/log/, CRACKZ_LOG_DIR env var

docs.title: ADR-007: Centralized CLI Options Pattern
docs.text:
Context: CLI option definitions were duplicated across modules (e.g., multiple FORCE_OPTION definitions).

Decision: Centralize all reusable CLI options in core/src/crackz/cli/options.py.

Consequences: - ✅ Single source of truth for option definitions - ✅ Consistent help text and behavior - ✅ Easy to update globally - ⚠️ Requires discipline to import (not re-define) - ⚠️ One-time refactoring effort to consolidate

Status: Active

Related: core/src/crackz/cli/options.py, all CLI commands

docs.title: ADR-008: Conventional Commits for Versioning
docs.text:
Context: Manual versioning and changelog generation is error-prone and time-consuming.

Decision: Use conventional commits (feat:, fix:, etc.) with semantic-release for automated versioning.

Consequences: - ✅ Automatic version bumps (major, minor, patch) - ✅ Auto-generated changelog from commits - ✅ Clear commit history for code review - ⚠️ Team must follow commit conventions - ⚠️ Bad commit messages affect release notes

Status: Active

Related: .releaserc.yml, GitHub Actions workflows

docs.title: ADR-009: Three Docker Variants (Full, Slim, GPU)
docs.text:
Context: Different deployment scenarios need different image sizes and capabilities.

Decision: Provide three Dockerfiles: - Dockerfile: Balanced full-featured image - Dockerfile.slim: Minimal runtime (no dev tools) - Dockerfile.gpu: CUDA runtime for GPU workloads

Consequences: - ✅ Optimized images for each use case - ✅ Faster pulls for slim (smaller size) - ✅ GPU support without bloating CPU images - ⚠️ Three Dockerfiles to maintain - ⚠️ Need clear documentation on which to use

Status: Active

Related: Dockerfile, Dockerfile.slim, Dockerfile.gpu, Makefile

docs.title: ADR-010: uv sync in Docker (Not Wheel Builds)
docs.text:
Context: Building wheels in Docker is slow and complex. uv sync is faster and simpler.

Decision: Use uv sync directly in Docker images instead of pre-built wheels.

Consequences: - ✅ Faster Docker builds (uv's speed) - ✅ Simpler Dockerfile (no multi-stage wheel building) - ✅ Consistent with local development workflow - ⚠️ Requires uv installed in base image - ⚠️ Build cache depends on pyproject.toml + uv.lock

Status: Active

Related: All Dockerfiles

docs.title: ADR-011: Ruff for Linting and Formatting
docs.text:
Context: Traditional Python linting (flake8, black, isort) requires multiple tools and is slow.

Decision: Use Ruff for both linting and formatting (replaces black, isort, flake8, etc.).

Consequences: - ✅ 10-100x faster than traditional tools - ✅ Single tool for linting + formatting - ✅ Compatible with existing configs (black, isort rules) - ✅ Excellent VS Code integration - ⚠️ Newer tool (less mature than black) - ⚠️ Some edge cases in AST-based fixes

Status: Active

Related: pyproject.toml (Ruff config), pre-commit hooks

docs.title: ADR-012: 75% Minimum Test Coverage
docs.text:
Context: Need quality gates without over-constraining development. 100% is unrealistic; <70% is too low.

Decision: Enforce 75% minimum test coverage in CI (target 85%).

Consequences: - ✅ Catches most untested code paths - ✅ Realistic target for teams - ✅ Enforced automatically in CI - ⚠️ Can be gamed with trivial tests - ⚠️ Doesn't measure test quality

Status: Active

Related: pyproject.toml (pytest-cov config), CI workflows

docs.title: ADR-013: Performance Regression Tests with Benchmarks
docs.text:
Context: Performance regressions are hard to catch without automated measurement.

Decision: Use pytest-benchmark with automated regression detection (>20% mean, >30% max).

Consequences: - ✅ Catches performance regressions before merge - ✅ Historical performance tracking - ✅ Baseline updates after intentional changes - ⚠️ Benchmark stability depends on CI environment - ⚠️ Requires baseline management

Status: Active

Related: tests/unit/benchmarks/, .benchmarks/ (gitignored)

docs.title: ADR-014: Project Schema Versioning with Migrations
docs.text:
Context: Project YAML format evolves over time. Breaking old projects is unacceptable for customers.

Decision: Add schema_version field to project configs with migration system.

Consequences: - ✅ Backward compatibility for customer projects - ✅ Explicit migration path for breaking changes - ✅ Safe upgrades (creates .bak files) - ⚠️ Migration code must be maintained - ⚠️ Testing migrations requires old project fixtures

Status: Active

Related: crackz migrate, core/src/crackz/config/, schema_version field

docs.title: ADR-015: typer.secho() for User Messages, logger for Technical Info
docs.text:
Context: Mixed output methods (print, echo, console.print) created inconsistent UX.

Decision: Standardize on: - typer.secho() with colors for end-user messages - logger for technical/operational information - NEVER use print(), typer.echo(), or console.print()

Consequences: - ✅ Consistent user experience across all CLI commands - ✅ Clear separation: user messages vs operational logs - ✅ Better testability (can capture typer output) - ⚠️ Requires team discipline to follow conventions - ⚠️ One-time refactoring effort to standardize existing code

Status: Active (strictly enforced)

Related: All CLI commands, CONTRIBUTING.md, DEVELOPMENT_STANDARDS.md

docs.title: ADR-016: GitHub Actions for CI/CD
docs.text:
Context: Need reliable, cloud-based CI/CD with good GitHub integration.

Decision: Use GitHub Actions exclusively (no Travis, CircleCI, etc.).

Consequences: - ✅ Native GitHub integration (PRs, issues, releases) - ✅ Free for public repos, generous for private - ✅ Good ecosystem of third-party actions - ✅ Matrix builds for multi-platform testing - ⚠️ Vendor lock-in to GitHub - ⚠️ YAML workflow syntax (learning curve)

Status: Active

Related: .github/workflows/

docs.title: ADR-017: MCP (Model Context Protocol) Integration
docs.text:
Context: AI assistants (Claude, Copilot) need standardized access to development tools.

Decision: Implement MCP integration with crackz mcp init command.

Consequences: - ✅ Standardized AI assistant integration - ✅ Fine-grained permission control - ✅ Future-proof for AI-powered development - ⚠️ Relatively new protocol (evolving spec) - ⚠️ Limited ecosystem currently

Status: Active

Related: core/src/crackz/cli/mcp_cli.py, .mcp/config.json

docs.title: ADR-018: GPS/EXIF Support with GeoJSON Export
docs.text:
Context: Harbor inspections often have GPS-tagged photos. Customers need location-based reports.

Decision: Add GPS extraction from EXIF, interactive maps (Folium), and GeoJSON export.

Consequences: - ✅ Location-aware detection results - ✅ Interactive HTML maps for visual reporting - ✅ GeoJSON export for GIS integration - ⚠️ Not all images have GPS data (graceful fallback) - ⚠️ Privacy considerations (GPS data in exports)

Status: Active

Related: crackz geo commands, core/src/crackz/geo/

docs.title: ADR-019: PySide6 Migration (Replacing CustomTkinter)
docs.text:
Context: CustomTkinter limitations became blockers for production use — limited widget set, no thread-safe state management, no native enabled/disabled widget support, customer requests for Qt (#127). A feasibility study confirmed PySide6 was viable under GPL-3.0 licensing.

Decision: Migrate GUI framework from CustomTkinter to PySide6 (Qt 6). Adopt reactive state management via QtAppState (QObject with signals) and Qt's thread-safe signal/slot mechanism via async_bridge.py.

Consequences: - ✅ Rich widget ecosystem (tree views, dock widgets, toolbars) - ✅ Native enabled/disabled widget support (setEnabled()) - ✅ Thread-safe signal/slot pattern — no manual locking for GUI state - ✅ Professional dark mode via Catppuccin Mocha QSS theming - ✅ Better packaging support (Qt deploy tools) - ⚠️ Larger dependency footprint (~50MB vs ~1MB) - ⚠️ Required full GUI rewrite (all views, dialogs, panels)

Status: Active

Related: gui/src/crackz_gui/qt/, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-04-13-pyside6-migration-feasibility.md, supersedes ADR-004

docs.title: ADR-020: Binary vs Multiclass as Distinct Task Modes
docs.text:
Context: For segmentation, projects with a single foreground category (crack vs. no-crack) and projects with multiple categories need different training and inference behaviour. The choice was: collapse both into one path (multiclass with N foreground classes, where N may be 1) or keep binary as a distinct task mode with its own head, loss, and mask-handling rules.

Crack-like defects are typically <1% of pixels. That class imbalance shapes what the model needs: - A tunable decision threshold (post-training precision/recall trade-off without retraining). - A loss that focuses on hard examples (focal loss).

Argmax over a 2-class softmax provides neither.

Decision: Keep binary and multiclass as distinct task modes, encoded via the TaskStrategy pattern in core/src/crackz/ai/model/segmentation/tasks.py. Auto-derive the mode from annotation.num_categories (1 → binary, >1 → multiclass), with explicit ai.model.task_mode override when needed. Persist task_mode and category_keys as checkpoint taxonomy metadata so checkpoints can be filtered for project compatibility (is_taxonomy_compatible).

Binary (num_categories == 1) Multiclass (num_categories > 1) Output 1 channel, sigmoid N+1 channels (incl. background) Decision tunable threshold argmax Loss Dice + Focal Dice + CE Metrics BinaryJaccardIndex, BinaryAccuracy MulticlassJaccardIndex w/ ignore_index=0, per-class IoU/Acc Mask tensor mask > 0 → float32 indexed → int64 Schema validation soft INFO warning for unusual uint8 values strict via validate_mask_label_ids

Consequences: - ✅ Threshold tuning available where it matters most (rare-foreground binary). - ✅ Focal loss directly addresses extreme class imbalance for binary; CE works fine when softmax balances multiple foreground classes. - ✅ Strategy pattern keeps CrackzModel free of per-mode if branches; adding a future mode (e.g. instance segmentation) is localised. - ✅ One-category projects can reuse multi-segment masks (e.g. GarayMC, values 2–254) — non-zero pixels collapse to foreground. - ⚠️ Two checkpoint-compat dimensions to track (task_mode + category_keys); paid for by taxonomy.py and a checkpoint-filter UI. - ⚠️ Binary-path masks are not schema-rejected (commit bfca877b, April 2026). This enables the GarayMC use case while preserving a breadcrumb for accidentally mismatched masks: Crackz logs once per dataset at INFO when binary-path mask values fall outside {0, 1, 255}. - ⚠️ Legacy checkpoints (task_mode=None, pre-schema-v6) are treated as binary by is_taxonomy_compatible. They appear compatible with any binary project but may still fail at load time; ensure_taxonomy_compatible warns rather than rejects.

Alternatives considered: - Always multiclass, with N=1 foreground. Rejected: loses sigmoid + threshold; loses focal loss; argmax over 2-class softmax provides no operating-point control after training. Net regression for the rare-defect domain that motivates this project. - Always binary, derived per category. Would require N independent models for multi-defect projects, duplicating training cost and losing the joint background discrimination that softmax+CE provides.

Status: Active

Related: core/src/crackz/ai/model/segmentation/tasks.py, core/src/crackz/ai/model/segmentation/model.py, core/src/crackz/ai/model/taxonomy.py, core/src/crackz/ai/data/dataset.py, PR #522
